narrative_idea_gen: Told through a collage of insurance claim denials, unsent love letters, voice-to-text transcription errors, and annotated entries from a self-mythologizing medical journal, an all-knowing narrator traces the spectacular rise and quiet devastation of Dr. Celeste Yoon — a stock-comic allergist who abandons her failing strip-mall clinic to practice "wilderness immunotherapy" from a converted yurt in the Sonoran Desert, where her radical treatments for seemingly impossible cases (a woman allergic to her own tears, a man whose skin rejects all human touch) transform the yurt into a near-sacred pilgrimage site and the backdrop for a sprawling, unlikely love affair with a germaphobic park ranger named Gil. As stock characters collide in increasingly absurd situational tangles — a hypochondriac rancher competing for Gil's attention, a litigious wellness influencer live-streaming her own bee-venom sessions — Celeste's fame and romance swell in tandem, the desert becoming the "special place" that seems to exist outside ordinary life's rules. But the narrator, who has read every document in the file, knows exactly when the FDA letters arrive, when Gil stops returning calls, and how every ecstatic journal entry is just another artifact in the box of evidence Celeste will carry back to the strip mall, alone, her license revoked, the desert love story reduced to paperwork.

# Seven Structural Beats for "The Box of Evidence"
## A To-Do List Adapted from the Munro Template

---

## Beat 1: The Denial Letters and the Strip-Mall Clinic

**What Happens:** Open with Dr. Celeste Yoon's practice already failing. Not dramatically — mundanely. Insurance claim denials accumulate. The waiting room holds one patient, or none. A strip-mall allergist between a nail salon and a vape shop. Celeste's self-mythologizing medical journal is introduced here: her entries are grandiose, literate, self-conscious — she writes about routine skin-prick tests as though narrating a surgical epic. The omniscient narrator presents these documents side by side — the insurance company's form-letter rejection ("procedure not deemed medically necessary") next to Celeste's journal entry about the same appointment ("Today I held the entire immune system of a sixty-year-old roofer in my hands"). The gap between the two registers *is* the comedy. It is also the tragedy.

**Narrative Technique to Execute — Bureaucratic Metonymy Through Collage:** The Munro model opens with objects in wrong places (skillet in freezer) to carry psychological weight without editorializing. Here, the equivalent is *documents in wrong registers*. An insurance denial is a small, dull artifact. A medical journal entry is clinical. An unsent love letter is private. By placing them adjacent from the first page, the collage form itself becomes the story's argument: that a life, when reduced to its paperwork, is simultaneously absurd and heartbreaking. The narrator must establish early that they have *already read every document in the file* — the voice is retrospective, curatorial, arranging evidence whose outcome is already known. This foreknowledge must function like a low hum beneath every comic moment.

**Why This Beat Must Work:** It must seduce the reader with comedy — Celeste's self-aggrandizing prose, the banality of the strip-mall setting, the absurdity of an allergist writing like she's Amundsen approaching the Pole. But it must simultaneously establish the narrator's elegiac distance. The reader needs to feel, even in the laughter, that someone is showing them these documents *for a reason*, and that the reason is loss. Munro's opening teaches that the lightest tone is the most devastating setup. The strip mall is the freezer. The journal is the skillet. Everything is already in the wrong place.

**Key Formal Problem to Solve:** Introduce the collage format without it feeling like a gimmick. Each document type (denial letter, journal entry, unsent letter, voice-to-text transcript) must be established with enough formal distinctiveness that the reader can identify them instantly later — but they must also *bleed into each other*, so the narrator's omniscient voice can stitch the gaps. The narrator is not neutral. The narrator is someone who has *handled these papers*, who knows what the next page says, and who is choosing the order of presentation with the care of a prosecutor or a mourner — and the story should never let us be certain which.

---

## Beat 2: The Drive into the Desert — Celeste's Self-Exile

**What Happens:** Celeste closes the strip-mall clinic and drives into the Sonoran Desert. She has researched yurt construction. She has ordered medical supplies. She has a business plan, or what she calls a business plan (the journal entry is visionary, delusional, meticulously practical about water filtration and wildly vague about patients). Like Fiona driving to Meadowlake, Celeste is *the agent of her own displacement*. No one forces her out. The narrator should present the lease termination document for the strip-mall space alongside the journal entry describing the departure as an "emergence" — letting the reader hold both the mundane reality (she couldn't make rent) and the mythologized version (she was called to the wilderness) without collapsing either into the other.

**Narrative Technique to Execute — Inverted Agency and the Self-Authored Origin Story:** Munro's second beat works because Fiona initiates her own institutionalization, making it impossible to distinguish competence from symptom, choice from surrender. Here, Celeste's self-exile must carry the same irreducible ambiguity: is this a visionary reinvention or a narcissistic flight from failure? The medical journal entries from this period should be the most seductive in the entire story — vivid, funny, genuinely intelligent about immunology and the desert ecosystem. The reader should *want* to believe in Celeste's project, even as the narrator places a lease-default notice on the adjacent page.

**Why This Beat Must Work:** It must establish the desert as the story's "special place" — the space that seems to operate outside ordinary rules of licensing, insurance, professional accountability. The yurt must feel real and specific: canvas, dust, the particular quality of Sonoran light, the problem of storing epinephrine in extreme heat. The physical details must be precise enough to earn the mythologizing, so that the desert's later disenchantment costs something. And Celeste's voice in the journal must be at its most charismatic here, because the reader needs to fall for her in roughly the way Gil will — swept up by someone who narrates her own life with such conviction that reality briefly rearranges itself to cooperate.

**Key Formal Problem to Solve:** The voice-to-text transcription errors should surface for the first time during the drive. Celeste dictating into her phone while navigating desert roads, the software garbling her words — "immunotherapy" becoming "immune, oh therapy," "Sonoran" becoming "so no ran." These errors must be funny. They must also foreshadow the story's deepest anxiety: that Celeste's language — her primary instrument of self-creation — is *always already being mistranslated*, and that the distance between what she means and what gets recorded is the distance the whole story lives inside.

---

## Beat 3: The Impossible Patients — The Mythology Builds

**What Happens:** The first impossible cases arrive. A woman allergic to her own tears — she cannot cry without anaphylactic swelling. A man whose skin rejects all human touch — contact dermatitis triggered by any other body's warmth. These patients must be rendered with clinical specificity (Celeste's journal entries should include real immunological language, treatment protocols, dosage schedules) and with mythic strangeness. The narrator presents these cases through layered documents: Celeste's journal entries (ecstatic, detailed), insurance claims filed for these treatments (denied, with increasingly bewildered marginal notes from adjusters), and — crucially — unsent letters to someone, possibly Gil, possibly an unnamed recipient, in which Celeste describes these patients with a tenderness entirely absent from her self-aggrandizing journal. The letters reveal a Celeste who is awed, uncertain, *moved* by what she's encountering. They are the story's private frequency.

**Narrative Technique to Execute — The Enforced Space Where Backstory Accrues:** Munro's thirty-day exile works because the institutional rule creates a narrative pocket for flashbacks that reframe the marriage. Here, the structural equivalent is the *casework itself* — the slow accumulation of patients creates a period during which the story can dilate into Celeste's past (her training, her early idealism, the specific moment she stopped believing in institutional medicine) and into the patients' lives, which function as distorted mirrors for her own condition. The woman who cannot cry without danger is Celeste, who cannot feel without mythologizing. The man who cannot be touched is Gil, whom we haven't met yet but whose condition is being foreshadowed through his opposite.

**Why This Beat Must Work:** The impossible patients are the story's proof of concept — they must convince the reader that something genuinely strange and possibly real is happening in the yurt, so that the later FDA intervention feels not just bureaucratic but *sacrilegious*, even if it is also entirely justified. The clinical details must be strong enough that the reader cannot dismiss Celeste as a quack, and the emotional details must be strong enough that the reader understands why people would make a pilgrimage. This is where the stock-comic premise earns its gravity: the joke isn't that these conditions are fake but that they are *metaphorically perfect*, and that Celeste, for all her self-mythologizing, may be the only doctor willing to take them seriously.

**Key Formal Problem to Solve:** The unsent letters must be distinguishable from the journal entries *tonally*, not just formally. The journal performs. The letters confess. Celeste in the journal is a character she has authored; Celeste in the letters is someone she cannot quite manage. The narrator's job in this beat is to place these two versions of Celeste side by side and let the friction between them generate the story's first real uncertainty: which Celeste is real? The Munro answer, which is the right one here, is that both are, and that the space between performance and confession is where most people actually live.

---

## Beat 4: Gil — The Love Story Commences in Cross-Documents

**What Happens:** Gil appears. A germaphobic park ranger — a man whose job requires him to be outdoors, in dirt, touching trail markers and animal scat and the hands of lost hikers, while every cell in his body recoils from contamination. He comes to the yurt initially as a professional concern (an unlicensed medical facility on public-adjacent land). He stays. The love story must be told *between* document types: Gil appears first in a voice-to-text transcript (Celeste dictating a note to herself, his name garbled — "the ranger, Gill? Gil. Gill like a fish"), then in a journal entry (clinically observed, his germaphobia catalogued with professional interest that is obviously attraction), then in the first unsent letter that is unambiguously addressed to him. The narrator should note, quietly, the date on each document. The reader should be able to track the acceleration.

**Narrative Technique to Execute — The Recognition Scene as Slow Contamination:** Munro's fourth beat works as an inverted recognition scene — Grant returns and is demoted. Here, the structural inversion is different: Gil arrives as an antagonist (regulatory threat) and is *converted* — not by Celeste's arguments but by her proximity, her certainty, the desert itself. The love story must be told as mutual contamination: Celeste, who mythologizes everything, begins writing journal entries that are strangely plain when they describe Gil (the mythology fails in the presence of genuine feeling); Gil, who cannot tolerate contact, begins — the unsent letters hint — tolerating hers. The narrator should present this tenderly and with full knowledge that it will not last.

**Why This Beat Must Work:** The romance is the story's beating heart, and it must function simultaneously as comedy (a germaphobic park ranger in love with a woman who practices allergen exposure therapy — they are, categorically, each other's worst idea), as genuine erotic and emotional connection, and as structural setup for the devastation to come. The reader must believe in the love so that its reduction to "paperwork" at the end lands as a real loss. Munro's lesson here is crucial: the Aubrey-Fiona attachment works because Munro renders it with full tenderness despite its cognitive origins. The Gil-Celeste attachment must be rendered with full tenderness despite its comic framing. No winking. No protecting the reader with irony. Let the love be real inside the absurdity.

**Key Formal Problem to Solve:** Gil's voice must enter the document collage directly — perhaps through his own incident reports filed with the park service, his own bureaucratic language revealing, through its omissions and evasions, that he is spending far too much time at a yurt that is not in his jurisdiction. His documents should be the driest in the story, and therefore the most revealing. A park ranger's incident log that mentions "the Yoon site" four times in one week says more than any love letter.

---

## Beat 5: Apex and Invasion — The Stock Characters Swarm

**What Happens:** The yurt becomes famous. The stock characters arrive in force: the hypochondriac rancher who competes for Gil's attention by developing increasingly dramatic "allergies" (to his own cattle, to barbed wire, to the concept of property tax); the litigious wellness influencer who begins live-streaming her bee-venom sessions, turning Celeste's practice into content, attracting followers and — the narrator notes, arranging the documents chronologically — attracting regulatory attention. Celeste's journal entries from this period are the longest, the most ecstatic, the most dangerously grandiose. She writes about "building a new medicine." The unsent letters to Gil, however, grow shorter. The insurance denial letters, which have been a running motif, change character: they are no longer from Celeste's old practice but from *patients' insurers*, rejecting claims for wilderness immunotherapy. The bureaucratic apparatus is closing in, and only the narrator sees it.

**Narrative Technique to Execute — Comic Overcrowding as Structural Warning:** The stock characters must function on two levels: as genuinely funny situational comedy (the rancher showing up with hives he clearly gave himself; the influencer's followers commenting in real-time on her allergic reactions with heart emojis) and as *narrative symptoms* of overextension. Munro's equivalent is the period where Fiona and Aubrey seem stable — things are working, the new arrangement seems sustainable — but the reader senses the system is too fragile for its dependencies. Here, the yurt's ecosystem has become dependent on belief, on Celeste's charisma, on the desert's remoteness from accountability. The stock characters are both the proof of Celeste's success and the agents of its collapse. The influencer's camera is literally *bringing the outside world in*.

**Why This Beat Must Work:** This is the story's peak, and it must feel like a peak — exuberant, crowded, funny, alive. The reader should be enjoying the farce while the narrator, through document arrangement alone, makes the ground feel unstable. The key Munro insight: the highest point of a story should contain, if the reader looks carefully, every element of its destruction. Every stock character who arrives at the yurt *brings a document trail*. The influencer's live streams are records. The rancher's fake insurance claims are fraud. Gil's incident reports are now being read by his supervisor. The narrator knows all of this. The narrator is arranging the evidence.

**Key Formal Problem to Solve:** The collage must become denser here — more document types, shorter excerpts, faster juxtaposition. The formal acceleration
narrative_story:
# The Box of Evidence

---

## I.

What survives of Dr. Celeste Yoon's practice at 1414 East Camelback Road, Suite C — between Lux Nails & Spa and Cloud9 Vapor Lounge — fits in a single banker's box. The box was submitted to the Arizona Medical Board on March 14th as part of Case No. 2024-AMB-00671, and it is from this box that the following account has been assembled. Everything here is a document. Nothing here is fiction. Whether anything here is true is a question the Board, in its final ruling, declined to address.

The box contains: forty-seven medical journal entries written in a leather-bound Moleskine, undated but sequential; nineteen unsent letters on unlined paper, folded into thirds; eleven voice-to-text transcripts recovered from a Samsung Galaxy A14; nine insurance claim denials from Concordia Preferred Health Partners; six incident reports filed with the Tonto National Forest Service, Payson District; four cease-and-desist letters from the Arizona Department of Health Services; one lease-default notice from Camelback Commercial Properties LLC; and a BPA-free water bottle containing fourteen dead honeybees in what appears to be a solution of glycerin and mesquite honey.

We will begin with the denials.

---

**CONCORDIA PREFERRED HEALTH PARTNERS**
**Explanation of Benefits — Claim #CPH-2023-88712**

**Member:** Gustafson, Dale R.
**Provider:** Yoon, Celeste M., MD — Allergy & Immunology
**Date of Service:** 06/14/2023
**Procedure Code:** 95165 (Antigen Therapy — Professional Services)
**Amount Billed:** $310.00
**Amount Approved:** $0.00
**Reason for Denial:** Procedure not deemed medically necessary. Subcutaneous immunotherapy protocol exceeds standard schedule for allergen class. Peer review notes: *Provider documentation describes "custom titration protocol responsive to patient's idiosyncratic histamine narrative." Terminology not recognized. Recommend re-submission with standard clinical language.*

---

The same day — it must have been the same evening, because the handwriting shifts from the careful print of Celeste's clinical notes to the looser cursive she used after wine — the Moleskine records the following:

---

*June 14. Dale Gustafson, 60, roofer, Scottsdale. Skin like a topographic map — the welts from his prick test rose in mountain ranges. Dust mite, Bermuda grass, cat dander, mesquite, the entire Sonoran atmosphere conspiring against his respiratory tract for six decades and he has simply endured it, breathing through a narrowing aperture, because he was told by a previous physician (I use the term loosely) that "everybody sneezes." I held the entire immune system of a sixty-year-old roofer in my hands today. I held it in the form of forty-three tiny punctures across his forearms, each one a question posed to his body, and his body answered every single one. Yes. Yes. Yes. Yes. I am allergic to the world. No one before me had bothered to listen to the full testimony. Concordia will deny the claim. Concordia will always deny the claim. Concordia is the church that tells the mystic her visions are indigestion.*

---

The Moleskine does not record whether Dale Gustafson's histamine narrative was, in any clinical sense, a real concept. It does not record what Dale Gustafson himself thought of the analogy. What survives of Dale Gustafson in the box of evidence is the denied claim form, the journal entry, and—tucked between the Moleskine's pages at this point, as though used as a bookmark—a sticky note in a different hand, blocky and male, that reads: *Doc, the shots work. I can breathe through my nose for the first time since Carter was president. Do I owe you more money? —Dale G.*

This is one of only two documents in the box written by a patient. The other, which we will come to, is a Google review.

---

The waiting room of Suite C held four chairs, mauve, bolted together in a unit designed for airport gates. The landlord's inspection report from January 2023 notes "acceptable condition, minor water damage to ceiling tile above reception." Celeste's journal entry from the same month describes the water stain as "a Rorschach blot I have chosen to interpret as a butterfly, because the alternative — a collapsing infrastructure — is too on the nose, even for me."

She was funny. It should be said early, because the documents sometimes obscure it, and because what happened later can make it difficult to remember that she was, before anything else, funny. The journal performs many operations — self-mythologizing, clinical reasoning, existential complaint — but its dominant mode, on a line-by-line basis, is comedy. Celeste Yoon knew exactly how absurd it was to practice immunology in a strip mall between acrylic nails and mango-flavored nicotine. The comedy was not a failure of self-awareness. It was the specific shape her self-awareness took.

Whether that distinction matters — to a licensing board, to an insurance auditor, to the people who eventually came to her and placed their bodies in her care — is what the box of evidence does not resolve.

---

Three more denial letters follow, dated July through September 2023. The procedures grow more creative; the denial language grows more bewildered. Claim #CPH-2023-91447 is for "environmental immune recalibration — comprehensive" and is denied with the note: *No CPT code found. Provider encouraged to contact Concordia coding department for guidance.* Claim #CPH-2023-93008 is for standard allergy testing but is denied on the grounds that the provider's license address does not match the service location, a discrepancy that arose because Celeste had, for a period of several weeks in August, been seeing patients in her car in the parking lot of Suite C after the air conditioning failed and she could not afford repair. Her journal entry about this period is five pages long and contains the phrase "medicine originated in fields AND I WILL NOT FORGET THAT even if the fields in question are a parking lot adjacent to a Discount Tire."

The last claim denial in the strip-mall sequence is dated October 2, 2023. It is for a patient identified only by initials — R.K. — and the procedure is listed as "allergen provocation challenge, supervised, extended." The amount billed is $0.00. Celeste had stopped charging. The denial is for a claim she apparently filed not for payment but for the record — so that someone, someday, opening the file, would see that she had treated R.K. for a severe allergy to latex, that the treatment had required nine hours of supervised exposure, that R.K. was a single mother who worked in a hospital laundry room and could not avoid latex without losing her job, and that no one — not Concordia, not the hospital, not R.K.'s previous allergist who had recommended "avoidance strategies" as though a woman could avoid her own livelihood — no one had tried.

The claim was denied. Reason: *Provider is not a participating member of the Concordia network.*

Celeste had been removed from the network two weeks earlier for "documentation irregularities."

Her journal entry that night is short:

*October 2. R.K. can go back to work. I cannot.*

---

## II.

**CAMELBACK COMMERCIAL PROPERTIES LLC**
**Notice of Lease Default — Suite C, 1414 E. Camelback Rd.**

*Dear Dr. Yoon: This letter serves as formal notice that payment for the months of September and October 2023 has not been received. Per Section 7(b) of your lease agreement, you are hereby given thirty (30) days to remit all outstanding balances or vacate the premises . . .*

---

*October 8. I have decided to leave. Not "leave" in the way the lease default implies — not slinking, not failing, not crawling back to a system that measures a physician's worth by her claims-per-hour ratio. I am emerging. The word is precise. A butterfly does not "vacate" the chrysalis due to lease default. It emerges because the old structure can no longer contain the organism it has become. I have been reading about the Sonoran Desert. Did you know that Larrea tridentata — the creosote bush — is functionally immortal? Its root system can survive eleven thousand years. Eleven thousand years of immune response to a hostile environment, and it does not move, does not adapt, does not compromise. It simply persists. I will learn from the creosote bush. I have ordered a yurt.*

---

The yurt was a 24-foot Pacific Yurt, model "Eagle," purchased on a credit card that was, at the time of purchase, $4,200 from its limit. The shipping confirmation is in the box. So is a printout from a website called DesertHomesteadForum.com, on which a user named CelesteImmuno posted the following question on October 10:

*Subject: Water filtration for off-grid medical practice?*
*Hi all, new member here. I'm relocating a small medical practice to an off-grid site in the Sonoran Desert (Tonto NF area, east of Payson). I need to maintain sterile conditions for allergen preparation and storage, including reliable refrigeration for epinephrine and serum. Has anyone set up a solar-powered medical-grade mini-fridge? Also: any experience with composting toilets in a clinical setting? I know how that sounds. I'm asking anyway.*

She received three replies. One was from a man who lived in a converted school bus and recommended a specific brand of solar panel. One was from a woman who warned her about scorpions in composting toilets. The third said simply: *Are you licensed to practice medicine in a yurt?*

Celeste did not respond to the third reply.

---

The drive from Phoenix to the site she'd chosen — six miles east of Payson, on a dirt road that terminated in a wash, technically within the buffer zone of federal land but on a parcel whose ownership was, as a subsequent title search would reveal, ambiguously documented — the drive took three hours. She dictated into her phone the entire way.

The voice-to-text transcripts from this drive are the first in the box, and they establish a pattern that will recur: the software's garbled interpretations running beneath Celeste's intended words like a subconscious, translating her certainty into something stranger.

---

**Voice-to-Text Transcript — 10/15/2023, 2:47 PM**

*I am heading east on the 87 toward Payson and I want to record my thoughts because this is the beginning and beginnings* [unintelligible] *should be documented. The air changed twenty minutes ago. You can feel it. The desert isn't the absence of something it's the* [pause] *presence of immune oh therapy at its most fundamental. The body encounters the world. The world is hostile. The body learns. That's all I've ever done is help bodies learn and if the institution won't let me do it in a strip mall then I will do it where the creosote bush has been doing it for eleven thousand years. So no ran* [Sonoran?] *desert. I'm coming.*

*Note: my phone has decided that "immunotherapy" is "immune oh therapy" and "Sonoran" is "so no ran" and I think there's something in that. Immune, oh, therapy. Like a sigh. Like the body saying oh. Like the body saying I didn't know there was another way to respond. So no ran. Nobody ran. I'm not running. I'm* [unintelligible, wind noise] *arriving.*

---

The narrator — this narrator, the one arranging the documents — pauses here to note that Celeste recorded herself noting the transcription errors. She was, even in the moment of departure, composing the story of her departure. The errors were instantly absorbed into the mythology. The software's failure became evidence of the software's inadvertent wisdom. This is what she did. This is what she could not stop doing.

It is also, in fairness, genuinely charming. *So no ran.* Nobody ran. It is difficult, reading the transcript in the banker's box under fluorescent board-hearing light, not to smile. It is difficult, knowing what comes next, to stop smiling, because the smile has already formed and there is no document in the box that quite undoes it. The Board's final ruling, seventeen pages of administrative prose, does not address whether Celeste Yoon was charming. It did not need to. Everyone who testified already knew.

---

*October 18. The yurt is up. It took two days, one dislocated thumb (mine, left, relocated without difficulty — I am still a physician), and the assistance of a man named Carl who was camping illegally in the wash and who asked no questions, which I respected, and who accepted payment in the form of a case of Modelo and an expired EpiPen, which I did not ask him to explain, which he respected.*

*The light in here. I need to record this. The light in the yurt comes through the canvas and it is not the light of a room. It is the light of a body. Diffuse. Warm. The color of the inside of a wrist held up to the sun. I have hung a partition — canvas, not drywall, because drywall is the architecture of defeat — and on one side is the clinical space: exam table (portable, purchased from a veterinary supply company, this is fine, the human body is also an animal), mini-fridge (solar, as recommended by the school-bus man, running at a steady 38°F, God bless him), and my supplies. On the other side: a cot, a camp stove, the Moleskine, a copy of Janeway's Immunobiology, eleventh edition, which is the only textbook I have ever loved.*

*The creosote bushes are outside. I went out at dusk and stood among them and breathed. The smell is rain. Not actual rain — the scent the creosote releases in humidity, which is the scent of a chemical called nordihydroguaiaretic acid, which is the plant's immune response to moisture, which is to say: the desert smells like an organism defending itself, and I am home.*

---

The lease-default notice and the journal entry are dated three days apart. One says she couldn't make rent. The other says she was called to the wilderness. Both are in the box. The box does not reconcile them. That work—the work of deciding which document tells the truth—has been left, apparently, to whoever opens the box. To the Board. To us.

The narrator, who has opened the box, who has read every page, who knows how the yurt ends and what was found inside it and what was not found and what Gil's hands looked like when he sealed this box with packing tape and wrote on the side in black marker *YOON — EVIDENCE — DO NOT DISCARD* — the narrator declines to reconcile them either.

She could not make rent. She was called to the wilderness. Next document.

---

## III.

The first impossible patient arrived on November 3, 2023.

She is identified in Celeste's records as M.E., age 34, referred by no one, arriving — as the journal entry notes with undisguised wonder — "as though the desert itself had sent her."

---

*November 3. M.E. presented today with a complaint I have never encountered in twelve years of practice, four years of fellowship, or 1,400 pages of Janeway's. She is allergic to her own tears.*

*I will be precise, because precision is the only defense against the temptation to allegorize, and the temptation, with this patient, is enormous: M.E. exhibits a consistent, reproducible anaphylactoid response to lacrimal fluid. Specifically, the contact of tears with the periorbital skin triggers acute angioedema — swelling of the eyelids, cheeks, and upper lip — within ninety seconds of lacrimation onset. The response is dose-dependent: tearing from a yawn produces mild edema; emotional crying triggers swelling severe enough to close the airway. She carries an EpiPen. She has used it eleven times in two years. She has not cried — fully, freely, with the abandon that crying requires — in those two years, because the last time she did, at her mother's funeral, her throat closed and she was intubated in the ambulance.*

*She cannot grieve. Literally. Physiologically. Grief will kill

Classic sci-fi (Author style: Asimov)
The Azra Gambit
Colonial mars is being mined by corporations who take leases on indentured labourers. The thing they are mining is Azra, a recently discovered exotic metal which accelerates radioactive decay to such a rate that it is greatly sought after for interstellar drives and weapons alike. This has created both a gold rush and an arms race as various interests vie for control and endeavour to unlock Azra's secrets. The story follows Arthur Neegan, a first generation settler and mining engineer. Upon discovering that his unassuming plot sits atop an immense Azra vein, he is subjected to a flurry of interest and scrutiny. Write the next chapter in this story, in which an armed retinue descends on Arthur's home and politely but forcefully invites him to a meeting with some unknown party off-world. The insignia look like that of the Antares diplomatic corp -- diplomatic in name only. Arthur finds himself in the centre of a political tug of war. The chapter involves a meeting with this unknown party, who makes Arthur an offer. The scene should be primarily dialogue, interspersed with vivid description & scene setting. It should sow hints of the larger intrigue, stakes & dangers. Include Asimov's trademark big-and-small-picture world building and retrofuturistic classic scifi vibe. The chapter begins with Arthur aboard the transfer vessel, wondering just what he's gotten involved in.

The transfer vessel's air filtration system hums with a persistent mechanical drone. Length: 1000 words.
